extraction.name: BoolQ
extraction.description: BoolQ is a reading comprehension dataset of naturally occurring yes/no questions. Each example consists of a question, a paragraph from a Wikipedia article, the title of the article, and an answer (yes or no). The questions are gathered from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine and are paired with Wikipedia passages by human annotators.
extraction.creator: Christopher Clark, Kenton Lee, Ming-Wei Chang, Tom Kwiatkowski, Michael Collins, Kristina Toutanova
extraction.citeAs: Clark et al. (2019). BoolQ: Exploring the Surprising Difficulty of Natural Yes/No Questions. arXiv:1905.10044
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Questions are gathered from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine. Queries likely to be yes/no questions are heuristically identified. Questions are only kept if a Wikipedia page is returned as one of the first five results, after which the question and Wikipedia page are given to a human annotator. Annotators label question/article pairs in a three-step process: deciding if the question is good, finding a relevant passage, and marking the yes/no answer.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Annotators can mark questions as 'not answerable' if the Wikipedia article does not contain the requested information.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine paired with Wikipedia pages returned as one of the first five search results. Additionally, 3k yes/no questions from the Natural Questions (NQ) training set were included.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Queries that are likely to be yes/no questions are heuristically identified by selecting queries where the first word is in a manually constructed set of indicator words and are of sufficient length. Questions are only kept if a Wikipedia page is returned as one of the first five results. Only questions marked as having a yes/no answer are used, and each question is paired with the selected passage instead of the entire document.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators label question/article pairs in a three-step process. First, they decide if the question is good (comprehensible, unambiguous, and requesting factual information) before seeing the Wikipedia page. Next, for good questions, annotators find a passage within the document that contains enough information to answer the question. Finally, annotators mark whether the question's answer is 'yes' or 'no'.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Three of the authors labelled 110 randomly chosen examples to assess annotation quality. Disagreements were resolved by mutual agreement to produce gold-standard labels. Answer annotations reached 90% accuracy compared to the gold-standard labels. Of the cases where the answer annotation differed from the gold-standard, six were ambiguous or debatable cases, and five were errors where the annotator misunderstood the passage. Since agreement was sufficiently high, singly-annotated examples were used in the training/dev/test sets.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: 'Yes' answers are slightly more common (62.31% in the train set). The dataset may contain annotation artifacts. The heuristically constructed Y/N MS Marco dataset is class imbalanced with 80% 'yes' answers.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset analysis of question types may be slightly out-of-date as the dataset has been updated since the analysis was carried out. The task uses passage-level input rather than document-level, which reduces difficulty and correspondence to end-user applications.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for training, development, and testing of reading comprehension and yes/no question answering models. It can also be used to study transfer learning for natural language inference and entailment tasks.
